job.style: a passage that shows a common wrong method and corrects it

response.passage: Rohan was studying symmetry for his math exam. He looked at a regular pentagon and claimed it only had one line of symmetry because he only drew a vertical line through the top vertex. His teacher explained that a regular pentagon has five lines of symmetry, one passing through each vertex and the midpoint of the opposite side. Next, Rohan looked at the letter 'P' in a mirror. He thought the reflection would look exactly like the original letter 'P'. However, he noticed the mirror image was flipped horizontally, appearing as a reversed 'P'. Rohan then rotated a square by 90 degrees. He initially believed that shapes only show symmetry when they complete a full 360-degree turn. His teacher corrected him, showing that the square looks identical to its original position after a 90-degree turn, which is less than a full circle. Finally, Rohan practiced drawing lines of symmetry on different shapes. He realized that lines of symmetry can be horizontal, vertical, or even diagonal, not just vertical lines. By understanding these concepts, Rohan learned that symmetry is about balance and transformation, not just one specific orientation or a single line. He now knows that shapes can have multiple lines of symmetry and rotational symmetry orders greater than one.
response.summary: Symmetry involves more than just vertical lines or full rotations. Regular polygons have multiple lines of symmetry, and mirror images are horizontally flipped. Shapes can also show symmetry through partial rotations.
